n: Daniel’s story begins around 605 BC, when Babylon’s young king Nebuchadnezzar first moved against Jerusalem. This was the first of several deportations; Ezekiel was taken later, in 597 BC, and the city fell in 586 BC.

f.g: Ruler of Babylon about 605–562 BC; his name is also spelled Nebuchadrezzar.

n: Daniel stresses that it was the Lord who handed Jehoiakim over—Babylon’s success was not a victory over God. Sacred temple vessels were carried to Babylon (Shinar) and placed in the temple of Nebuchadnezzar’s god as trophies.

f.w: the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand

f.g: An ancient name for the region of Babylonia, where the tower of Babel was built.

f.w: vessels of the house of God

n: Nebuchadnezzar orders Ashpenaz, his chief official, to select young men from Judah’s royal family and nobility. Training captive elites was a way to build loyal administrators. Isaiah had foretold that royal descendants would serve in Babylon’s palace.

f.g: Chief court official; the title may simply mean palace officer.

n: Only the best were chosen: physically flawless, good-looking, intelligent, and well-educated. They would learn the language and literature of the Chaldeans—Babylon’s learned class.

f.g: Here, Babylon’s scholarly class of astrologers and scribes; elsewhere the name of the people.

n: The students receive food and wine from the king’s own table for a three-year course. Eating the king’s food signaled dependence and loyalty to him.

f.g: Fine food or delicacies from the royal table; “meat” = food in KJV English.

n: Among the young men from Judah were four friends: Daniel (“God is my judge”), Hananiah (“the Lord is gracious”), Mishael (“who is like God?”), and Azariah (“the Lord has helped”). Each Hebrew name honors the God of Israel.
They are given Babylonian names, many tied to Babylonian gods—an attempt to reshape their identity. Belteshazzar likely means “protect the king’s life,” invoking the god Bel.

f.g: A Babylonian name probably meaning “(Bel) protect his life.”
“Servant of Nego,” likely a play on the god Nabu.

n: Daniel made a firm decision in his heart not to defile himself with the king’s food and wine. The food may have violated the Law of Moses or been offered to idols. His courage begins with a quiet, private resolve.
God gave Daniel favor and compassion in the official’s eyes. Daniel’s faithfulness is matched by God’s quiet help behind the scenes.

f.w: God had brought Daniel into favour

n: The official fears that if the young men look unhealthy, the king will blame him—and he could lose his head. His worry is practical, not hostile.
Daniel approaches the guard assigned to them. “Melzar” may be a title meaning “guardian” or “steward” rather than a personal name.
Daniel proposes a respectful, reasonable test: ten days of simple vegetables and water. He offers a solution rather than a demand.

f.g: Vegetables, legumes, or seeds—simple plant food.

n: “Compare us after ten days, then decide.” Daniel trusts God for the results.
The steward agrees to the trial.
After ten days, the four look healthier and better nourished than those eating the royal food. God honors obedience—echoing the Word of Wisdom’s promise of health.
The steward permanently replaces their royal rations with vegetables.
God gives the four young men knowledge and wisdom, and Daniel receives a special gift: understanding of visions and dreams. That gift sets up the rest of the book.

f.w: Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams

n: After three years of training, the students are presented to Nebuchadnezzar.
The king interviews them himself, and none compares with these four. They are given positions in the royal court.
In every question the king asks, they prove ten times wiser than all his magicians and astrologers. God’s gifts surpass Babylon’s best learning.

f.g: Babylon’s experts in omens, dream interpretation, and divination.

n: Daniel served in Babylon until the first year of Cyrus (about 539 BC), when Persia conquered Babylon—more than sixty years. He outlasted the whole empire that had taken him captive.

f.w: the first year of king Cyrus
